label: text
text: But this claim, which is contested by Spain on the ground that the latter's Protectorate can be legitimately exercised without necessarily involving a complete military occupation (as a matter of fact, within the French zone the military frontier does not everywhere extend as far as the political frontier), is to be upheld, for the time being, rather on abstract than on practical grounds. In effect, the present

label: text
text: Although to-day's cables from Morocco report that the Riffs have "infiltrated" into the French zone, the position need not be viewed with any due alarm. Marshal Lyantey is confident he can deal with the trouble with the troops at his disposal. The intentions and dispositions of the French Government, there is every reason to believe, are as pacific towards the Riffians as they are conciliatory towards Spain, and considerate of her susceptibilities. France, it is true, maintains her legal interpretation of the Franco-Spanish Agreements of 1904 and 1912 as investing Spain with the duty, as well as the right, to control effectively the Moroccan zone entrusted to her protectorate, i.e., to ensure by a military occupation that no troubles shall occur within that zone such as might entail any danger to the adjoining French zone. Juridically, therefore, France would claim for herself the right to occupy militarily any areas evacuated by the Spanish army with resultant difficulties to the contiguous frontier regions of the French Protectorate.

label: text
text: French Government and Chamber, and it is assumed, the great bulk of French public opinion, are resolutely opposed to any territorial extension of the French Protectorate and to any additional military liabilities. Accordingly, it is sincerely hoped and believed that Abd-el-Krim will not be so rush as to seek a serious quarrel with the neighbouring French authorities by incursions into French-protected areas, but will be content to let alone and be let alone.

label: text
text: From the British and international standpoint, what really matters, is the status of the Riffian coast, because of its proximity to Ceuta, Tangier, and the Straits of Gibraltar. The extreme reticence on this subject manifested by Mr. Austen Chamberlain in the course of his recent statement at Westminster was no doubt due to his appreciation of the delicate nature of the problem, which might at any time become critical. Similarly, although the Moroccan question was touched upon by the British Foreign Secretary in the course of his conversations with M. Herrict and Signor Mussolini, Mr. Chamberlain, so it was gathered from both capitals, was too tactful and discreet to enter fully into the matter with either party in the absence of the third. If and when circumstances should warrant an international discussion of the Moroccan problem in all its aspects, the British attitude will naturally be openly and more clearly defined.

label: text
text: Shanghai—or a firm there—sets an example that might well be followed by business houses in Hongkong. Messrs. Jardine, Matheson & Co., Ltd., have decreed that during the summer months their business hours are to be 8.30 a.m. to 12 noon and 2 p.m. to 4.30 p.m. The summer is as trying in Shanghai as it is in Hongkong. An early start, an extended tiffin interval and an early cessation of work probably means greater productivity although the actual working hours are less. A good start is the main thing and a man is more likely to be eager for his work at 8.30 a.m., than he is at 9 a.m., be the difference only thirty minutes. It may be that productivity is not the thing aimed at, but simply a realisation that Europeans work at a disadvantage in the torrid, or humid conditions of a Far Eastern summer, a recognition of that fact, and the introduction of a system that aims at a condition of things which shall be to the advantage of the European and a means to strengthen his reserves of health. It is about time such a sensible system be adopted by Hongkong business houses.

label: paragraph_title
text: May Day:

label: text
text: It is not clear why the organised forces of Labour have selected the first day of May on which to celebrate their existence and to voice their grievances—fancied or real. The Morris pole is, presumably forsaken, and processions of drabness and speeches of spleen, take its place. London's labourists march to the Bulgarian Legation and protest against the alleged persecution of Bulgarian workers—a persecution which is denied. Moscow's "joy" is more militaristic than Labouristic. There the garrison is reviewed, 50 aeroplanes participate, the while members of the Government and Diplomatic Corps look on. Canton provides the humour, although it is stud and sorry stuff. "Down with foreign religion," and "Down with capitalism" are the cries, whilst there is a word for the "progressive Soviet." The Cantonese dearly love a procession. The one at Canton was three miles long. There is something pathetic about these processions—in London, Moscow and Canton. We do not seem to have progressed very far even in China with its boasted civilisation, when a three-mile long procession can give vent only to parrot like cries the purport of which, it seems very likely, at least one and half miles of the procession does not understand.

included in a list of

Three days in the year on which no business must be started, according to a noble Lord in 1633, were the first Monday in April, the second Monday in August and the last Monday in December. The first because it was then that Cain was born, and also the day on which he killed his brother; the second because that was the day on which the cities of the plain were destroyed; and the third because it was the birthday of Judas Iscarot I.

THE GREEN
GODDESS.

label: text
text: There has been a trek to the World Theatre to see "The Green

label: text
text: Goddess." Some of us have gone to see the film; because we have read the play; others because the late William Archer wrote it. It is a good film and the Americans, who did it, are to be congratulated. George Arliss makes a fine Rajah. And George Arliss is English acting in American movies; whilst in the story Americans give fine impersonations of English characters. Another item of interest is a "shocker" of a play written by an intellectual and one of the finest gentlemen and critics that England has produced. Such films as this one make the cinema possible. There is hope.

label: paragraph_title
text: ANIMALS AT THE OPERA

label: text
text: Hongkong is a place -fit for heroes to live in. Read this ue of the Straits

label: text
text: from a recent issue of the Straits Times:—

label: text
text:
Sir,—We are alas, some what accustomed to lax manners in the audiences at the Victoria Theatre but I venture to suggest we have about reached the limit when animals are allowed inside at an operatic performance. The admirable performance of La Traviata was marred by the yapping of a pet dog carried by some one in the stalls, and the chattering of a pet monkey brought by a lover of music into the circle. In addition those in the circle were compelled to listen to the incessant buzz of conversation which hardly ever died away throughout the entire performance, and which emanated from one corner of the circle only.
In a London theatre one could complain to a stalwart attendant who would speedily amend matters, but in Singapore one can only suffer in silence.—Yours etc.

text: THE ABBEY WAXWORKS.

label: text
text: Although Tussaud's is said to be the oldest waxwork collec-

label: text
text:
tion in Europe, there existed long before a chantry in Westminster Abbey containing effigies of princes and nobles who were buried in the Abbey. By 1754 the relics were so ancient that the robes of Edward VI had turned from rich crimson-volvet to a semblance of russet leather. All the best preserved costumes had been stripped from the effigies, which were sadly mistreated in the handling.
WAX AND THE GUILLOTINE.
It was the French Revolution that founded Ma-

label: text
text: dame Tussaud's Chamber of Horrors. In pursuit of her realistic art she did not hesitate to take models direct from heads severed by the guillotine to enrich her first collection, which was established on the Boulevard du Temple, Paris, in 1780. Her family for four generations came near making a longevity record, herself, her mother, grandmother and great-grandmother totalling five years short of four hundred.

label: paragraph_title
text: In the Daily Express "Beachcomber" writes: Mr. Robert Lynd is re-

label: text
text: ported to have said that he finds it impossible to imagine anybody writing a good poem about tripe. I disagree. Many of our younger poets have written poems so realistic that they were actually mistaken for tripe. itself. And, anyhow, I myself will at once write a good poem about tripe. Here it is:

label: text
text:
Come, gentle tripe, the hungry
carter's joy.

label: text
text:
Drayman's delight, conductor's second course,
Passion and dream of every errand-boy,
Vision of every rogue that holds a horse,
Bane of all titled ladies, bishop's dread,
Doorn of the softly nurtured, peers' despair,
Was it for this the tall Achilles bled,
For this that Agamemnon tore his hair?
Was this the food that launched a thousand ships
And tore the heart of Dido, as she stood
Above the feast, wiping her royal lips,
And called her love again—was this food?
The answer is, in a sense, no.
